newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Debre wants blocks on illegal immigration.
newsitem.headline: France's Debre wants blocks on illegal immigration.

text.p: Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre said in an interview released on Monday he wanted a total halt to illegal immigration into France where there are about a million illegal migrants among five million foreigners.

"I am for zero illegal immigration. The state must be given the means to dissuade those foreigners who want to enter France without resources, papers or jobs," Debre told daily newspaper Le Parisien in an interview to be published on Tuesday.
The "zero illegal immigration" concept is controversial in France. Civil liberty groups say Paris has a moral duty as an ex-colonial power to allow some influx from developing countries.
They say "zero immigration" is inhuman and contrary to France's image as a land of asylum.
They argue that former Socialist administrations issued periodic amnesties for illegal migrants who generally then integrated well into society, performing jobs which native French people shunned.
Debre, a Gaullist, denied his policy would encourage rightist Jean-Marie Le Pen's National Front party which wants to expel millions of legal immigrants from France.
"It is by refusing to tackle the problems of our country that one helps the National Front," he said.
Debre will seek tougher immigration laws in a new parliamentary debate on Tuesday.
Proposed amendments to the law include doubling to two years the period before which the foreign spouse of a French national receives permanent residency rights.

Police officers say this will halt the traffic in fake weddings where foreigners offer money to poor French people to marry them, allowing them enter the country legally, then divorce and bring their own families to France.
The immigration issue led to nationwide controversy last summer when police forcibly evicted over 200 Africans, mostly illegal immigrants, from their refuge in a Paris church.
Magistrates later overturned government orders expelling most of them on technical grounds and the new laws Debre wants would prevent a repeat of the situation.

"Between those who back laxness and those who want segregation, between those who want a multi-cultural society and those who want a xenophobic country, there is a road of reason," said Debre, adding that toughened laws would protect those immigrants who entered France legally.
Debre said he was wary of introducing immigration quotas, like those in the United States, because this could cause diplomatic problems with France's ex-colonies in Africa.
